The incident occurred near the village of Salcia in Romania’s Mehedinți County, close to the border with Bulgaria. There are 186 passengers and 52 crew members on board. The vessel departed Monday evening from the Romanian city of Drobeta-Turnu Severin and was heading to Vidin, Bulgaria, but became stuck on a sandbar and was unable to continue its journey. According to authorities, the water level in the Danube remains extremely low: the river’s flow is about 1,600 cubic meters per second, which significantly complicates navigation. Attempts to refloat the ship made on Monday evening and Tuesday morning were unsuccessful. Representatives of the river administration acknowledged that the chances of freeing the vessel quickly are slim. Later, Bulgaria’s border police began evacuating the passengers. As the country’s Interior Ministry reported, the cruise ship was also running low on drinking water ahead of a scheduled stop at the port of Vidin to replenish supplies. Another boat was brought in to transport the people, but it was unable to get close enough to the stranded vessel. As a result, passengers wearing life jackets were transferred on border police patrol boats. There have been no reports of injuries. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62j.text: Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images Image caption, The father was given a fast-tracked hearing in Toulouse By Paul Kirby Europe digital editor Published 16 minutes ago A man has been given a six-month jail term in France after he threatened to kill a female primary school teacher who had disciplined his son at a village primary school. He was sentenced after a fast-track hearing on Thursday, six days after the events unfolded in Le Fauga, a village with a population of about 2,600 just outside the southwestern city of Toulouse. The teacher has been granted official protection and has gone on sick leave. French Education Minister Edouard Geffray said: "No teacher should be afraid to do their job. Attacking one of them is attacking the entire institution." Over the summer, Geffray steered through a law aimed at protecting staff from a "significant risk" to their safety or health from a member of a student's family. The minister said this case would trigger one of the first uses of the decree. The case revives terrible memories in France of the beheading of a teacher in the Paris suburb of Conflans-Sainte-Honorine six years ago. Samuel Paty was murdered outside his school by an 18-year-old Chechen refugee. In Le Fauga, the teacher's colleagues did not go into work on Monday because of what had happened the previous Friday. The threat was made after the man had been called in for a chat with the school, according to Toulouse education chief Karim Benmiloud. Le Fauga Mayor Jean-Marie Puig told BFMTV that the man's son had been disruptive in class and the teacher had sent him to another class to calm down, although he continued to misbehave. The teacher in this class was alleged to have told the child to "stop acting like a little bully", BFMTV reports. She was then threatened by the father, who according to the mayor had waited for her "outside the school and apparently threatened to cut off her head if she'd been a man". The parent subsequently apologised, however a judicial complaint was made and he went before the prosecutor in Toulouse on Thursday afternoon. The decree passed in July allows for a student to be transferred to another school in a case involving significant risk to staff, and where education authorities have intervened. It is thought the boy and a younger sister may now be moved to another school outside Le Fauga. https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/eur.text: IMarEST: From MASS Code to Maritime Practice Ship Recycling Markets Remain Active Coal in Focus — China’s 2027–28 US Coal Commitment Baltic Index Falls for 3rd Session Intergr8 Fuels: Global fuel quality remains broadly stable, but localised risks are becoming more important than headline averages European countries urge for joint policy action to tackle soaring oil prices in Oil & Companies News 24/09/2026 European leaders have called for joint policy action, including relaxed fuel quality standards and revised biofuels regulations, to help bring fuel costs down from record highs ahead of the peak winter demand season. Since the latest flare-up in the Middle East conflict, Europe has seen fuel costs set fresh record highs, sparking concerns over affordability in the months when supplies are typically compressed by a shift to winter fuel specifications. In a statement on Sept. 22, a spokesperson for the European Commission confirmed that Commission President Ursula von der Leyen had received a letter from France’s President, Emmanuel Macron, regarding potential responses to the crisis. The spokesperson said that the commission would “reply in due course,” without providing further detail on the content of the letter. Calls for tougher policy action were echoed by Slovakian Prime Minister Robert Fico, who criticized the bloc for its failure to address “astronomic” fuel prices and called for a special EU summit on coordinated action. Speaking at a press conference in Bratislava, Fico blamed a lack of joint EU measures for impacting the welfare of European citizens through the crisis, and urged Brussels to come up with new measures to help manage the economic impact. Regional governments have already introduced a patchwork of emergency measures to try and limit price hikes and prioritize the domestic market. Concerned about “diesel tourism,” from neighboring countries, Slovakia banned diesel exports and set higher prices for foreign motorists earlier in the year. On Sept. 21, the Czech government announced it would reintroduce diesel and gasoline price caps in the retail sector, and joined Poland in announcing special taxes on refinery profits. After the US-Iran conflict erupted in late February, the International Energy Agency cautioned that emergency fiscal measures can prove costly for governments and challenging to phase out, and emphasized demand-side measures such as lower speed limits and work-from-home directives as ways to slash fuel use. As members of the IEA, which includes most EU countries, nations are expected to devise emergency action plans to address supply disruptions, potentially including fuel rationing and the relaxation of fuel quality standards. France delays winter spec change In an example of unilateral action, France announced in its official government journal on Sept. 22 that it would authorize the domestic sale of summer-specification diesel until Nov. 15, two weeks later than its usual Nov. 1 deadline, citing supply difficulties due to the Middle East crisis. Among his recommendations to the European Commission, Macron called for wider revisions to diesel and jet fuel specifications across the bloc, French media reported, citing expectations the pivot could boost output of the two fuels by up to 20%. Additionally, the letter was reported to have suggested measures to increase the quantity of biofuel that can be blended into diesel for automotive use, potentially lifting blending constraints from the current 7% (B7) threshold. Representatives for the French Presidency did not respond to a request for comment. Xavier Noyon, Secretary General of the European Biodiesel Board, welcomed the potential measure, and reiterated calls for a higher 10% limit in the passenger vehicle sector. “Fewer restriction[s] will mean faster decarbonization, and the European biofuel sector is ready to deliver,” he said. Should the proposal move ahead, higher blending limits could prove supportive of Europe’s growing biodiesel market, which has become increasingly economical compared to gasoil. According to assessments from Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, European FAME 0 biodiesel commanded a $310/mt premium to ICE Low Sulfur Gasoil futures on Sept. 21, down from $553/mt before the conflict began. France currently holds the G7 presidency, and Macron told a Paris press conference Sept. 18 that he would call a meeting among its member states to discuss further oil stock releases. The bloc backed a 400 million barrel stock release coordinated by the International Energy Agency, which was announced in March and was 75% complete as of Sept. 18. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmvg.text: Image source, @nayibbukele Image caption, El Salvador's president posted a video on X of the strikes on a complex he said is the headquarters of 400 Mawozo By Will Grant ,Â Central America correspondent Â and Â Claire Keenan Published 1 hour ago The headquarters of one of Haiti's largest crime gangs has been destroyed by El Salvador's military, the Salvadoran president has said. The infamous 400 Mawozo gang, which is known for kidnappings and intimidation tactics, was targeted in a ground and air attack at a complex on the outskirts of Haiti's capital, Port-au-Prince. It is El Salvador's first military action on a Haitian target since it deployed more than 2,000 soldiers there last month, as part of a mission to rescue four missing Salvadoran technicians. Haiti has been plagued by gang violence for years, with heavily armed groups controlling large parts of the capital, and beyond. El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele announced the news on X , external , boasting that most of the gang members fled without trying to fight. "We destroyed the house of [gang leader] LanmÃ² San Jou and the 400 Mawozo gang's headquarters," he wrote on Tuesday. The post was accompanied by video of several helicopters firing on a large complex, reportedly in the suburb of Croix-des-Bouquets, the gang's stronghold. As the helicopters circle above, dozens of people can be seen running out of the property, fleeing the strikes. Several media outlets have reported that as many as 20 people were killed, however that has not been confirmed by authorities. There has also been no official confirmation of the extent of the damage at the property, with Haitians questioning whether it has been destroyed or just damaged. The Miami Herald reports that the gang's leader, Wilson "LanmÃ² San Jou" Joseph, was not there at the time. The BBC has not been able to verify the video posted by Bukele, nor whether the property is indeed the gang's headquarters. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Salvadoran troops have become a regular sight in Port-au-Prince Haiti's National Police drone task force was involved in the attack, supported by Salvadoran soldiers, the Miami Herald reports, citing several sources. Posting on X after the strikes, Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-AimÃ© thanked the Salvadoran military's commitment "in the fight against gangs", and said the two nations would keep working together, along with the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), to "regain control of the territory and restore state authority". "THE GANGS WILL GET NO SLEEP!" he added. Some 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers were deployed to Haiti last month after four air force technicians were abducted at gunpoint while food shopping in October. El Salvador's right-wing president has vowed to bring the men home alive and warned the gang to release them immediately or face sustained pressure from his military. The four abducted men were working as part of the GSF, made up of troops from several nations, initially led by soldiers from Chad. President Bukele's move to send thousands of Salvadoran troops to Haiti has raised concerns, with critics saying they are not all working within the command structure of the GSF. It has raised questions about the operational legitimacy and legality of their actions in the Caribbean nation. Amnesty International has urged both countries to "ensure all operations conducted by Salvadoran forces in Haiti comply with international human rights law". Such concerns do not appear to phase Bukele, however, who continues to directly warn and target the gang leaders. The attack on the supposed gang headquarters seemingly came after a user on X had urged Bukele to attack the complex. "Where is that house? Give us the exact address, and we'll destroy it," he replied to the post, which has now been taken down, apparently for violating X's rules. The 400 Mawozo gang is the largest criminal organisation in Haiti, and known for kidnappings, extortion, murders and arms trafficking. Haiti is the poorest country in the Americas and remains largely under gang control. At least 5,700 people have been killed or injured there by gangs or during operations against them between 1 January and 11 September this year alone, the United Nations has said. El Salvador has recorded huge reductions in gang violence under President Bukele as part of a sweeping crackdown, and he has vowed to do the same in Haiti. However, human rights groups have argued that the way he has done it is unlawful, with the open-ended extension of emergency laws, the treatment of detainees in El Salvador's high-security mega-prison and the mass trials of alleged gang members.
